definition: A spot on the lung, smaller than 3 centimeters (or less than 30 millimeters), that looks different from surrounding normal lung tissue on imaging tests.
general_symptoms: Small lung nodules rarely cause symptoms
Chronic cough or coughing up blood
Loss of appetite and unexplained weight loss
Recurring respiratory infections like bronchitis or pneumonia
risk_factors: Smoking or past history of smoking
Family history or personal history of cancer
Past radiation therapy to the chest
Exposure to asbestos, radon, or secondhand smoke
general_diagnosis_methods: CT scan (including active surveillance every 6 to 12 months)
Blood tests (to look for infections or other causes)
Sputum tests (to look for infections or other causes)
Tissue sample (biopsy) including Bronchoscopy, Thoracoscopy, Video-assisted thoracic surgery (VATS), and Needle biopsy
general_treatments: Small, noncancerous lung nodules usually don't require treatment
Active surveillance with additional imaging in 6 to 12 months
Medications for infection-caused nodules (antibiotics or antifungal medications)
Surgery (if the nodule grows, causes symptoms, or blocks an airway)
life_expectancy: Most pulmonary nodules aren't harmful and don't affect survival
If cancerous, survival rate depends on cancer type and stage
general_outlook: Most lung nodules are benign (not cancerous)
Benign nodules will usually stay the same size or go away on their own
Nodules staying the same size during a two-year surveillance period are unlikely to be cancer
Nodules smaller than 0.6 cm and those with smooth edges are less likely to be cancerous
Nodules <5 mm have a <1% chance of being cancerous
Nodules 5 mm to 10 mm have up to a 28% chance of being cancerous
Nodules >2 cm (approaching lung mass size) have a 64% to 82% chance of malignancy
Nodules can sometimes begin to grow
complications: Pressing against or blocking an airway (rare for noncancerous nodules)
prevention: Not much can be done to prevent benign nodules
Quitting smoking to keep lungs healthy
living_with: Follow up with healthcare provider for additional tests or surveillance
Monitor for symptoms like shortness of breath or chronic cough
Seek ER/911 for chest pain, difficulty breathing, or coughing up blood

causes_by_type.description: Clusters of immune cells; the most common kind of benign nodules.
Noninfectious nodule formations caused by autoimmune conditions.

types: Atypical adenomatous hyperplasia (condition that can lead to cancer)

causes: Breathing in lung irritants and chemicals

structural_classification.description: Area is hazy and structures underneath remain visible.
Combination of solid and ground-glass opacity.

definition: An abnormal area in the lungs larger than 3 centimeters (about 1.5 inches). More likely to be malignant compared to a lung nodule.
risk_factors: Environmental/occupational exposure to cancer-causing agents (e.g., radon, asbestos, wood dust in carpenters)
general_causes: Metastatic cancer from other body parts (breast, colon, bladder cancer)
general_diagnosis_methods: Bronchoscopy (with or without Endobronchial ultrasound for central mass near large airways)
Fine needle biopsy (for mass in outer lung regions)
Thoracic surgery / Lung surgery (Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery [VATS] or traditional thoracotomy)
general_treatments: Treatments specific to non-cancerous causes (e.g., for infections based on specific diagnosis)
life_expectancy: Advances in treatment have extended survival times in recent years
general_outlook: Most often diagnosed as lung cancer (especially with a history of smoking)
More concerning if described as 'ground glass' on imaging
Typically benign if stable for two years
Benign tumors are more likely if showing calcifications, fat, or cavitary shapes
complications: Some benign causes can cause serious health complications

types: Non-small cell lung cancer (85% of lung cancers; includes adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, large cell carcinoma)
Small cell lung cancer (10% to 15% of lung cancers)

subtypes.details: Includes hamartoma (most common type). People with Cowden syndrome have greater risk.
Infections walled off and contained by the body.
Abnormal connection between arteries and veins usually present from birth.
Outpouching in arteries traveling from heart to lungs.
Build-up of abnormal proteins forming a mass.
